::: {.kw-overview}
Two papers this week argue that we have been counting HLA mismatches when we should be classifying them. A five-centre study of three thousand recipients shows that HLA-DQ alleles fall into two evolutionary clades and that crossing between them carries a directional risk of de novo donor-specific antibody and antibody-mediated rejection which the fashionable amino-acid-level quantitative metrics fail to see, and a Quebec cohort independently finds that the donor's DQ heterodimer group predicts graft loss irrespective of DQ and DR mismatch counts — a categorical, biologically grounded alternative to eplet arithmetic that arrives from two directions at once. Preservation supplies the second theme, and all three papers treat the perfusion circuit as something more than a fridge: perfusate cell-free DNA, and specifically its mitochondrial fraction, tracks post-transplant function during both hypothermic and normothermic perfusion though in the opposite direction to intuition; the first US comparative series of end-ischemic hypothermic oxygenated perfusion reports better one-year function than non-oxygenated perfusion despite preservation times approaching twenty-eight hours; and an unsupervised clustering analysis of the entire UK registry locates machine-perfused cases within six data-derived donor-recipient phenotypes rather than in a category of their own. Donor utilisation and access appear in a mandatory US payment experiment whose first nine months produced a measurable divergence in deceased donor transplant volume between randomised and non-randomised centres, and in a Chinese cohort quantifying the kidney failure and mortality risk carried by hepatitis B surface antigen-positive living donors. The issue closes on the long game, with thirty years of linked Australasian death registrations showing that keratinocyte cancer, not melanoma, is what actually kills kidney transplant recipients with skin disease — a thirty-four-fold excess that should reorder how we run surveillance clinics.
:::

---

### 1. [A multicenter kidney transplantation study identifies hierarchy and directionality of HLA-DQ alloimmune responses](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-76912-7)
[Van Den Broek DAJ, Agrawal A, Crespo M, Emonds MP, Heidt S, van der Helm D, Lenz TL, Meneghini M, Palou E, Redondo Pachón D, Roelen DL, Senev A, Naesens M, de Vries APJ, Tambur AR. *Nat Commun*, 2026. PMID: 42749717.]{.kw-ref}

Histocompatibility has spent the past decade moving from counting serologic mismatches to counting mismatched amino acids, and this study argues that the second approach inherits the conceptual error of the first by treating immunogenicity as a quantity when it behaves like a category. The authors applied hierarchical clustering to HLA-DQ αβ-heterodimers using HLA evolutionary divergence together with the physiochemical properties of the constituent amino acids, and found that DQ alleles segregate into two principal evolutionary clades which subdivide further into six functional sub-categories. Applying that stratification to 3,003 kidney allograft recipients across five transplant centres, they show that transplantation across the two clades generates humoral responses with both a hierarchy and a direction — meaning the risk depends on which clade the recipient sits in and which the donor's antigen came from, not merely on how far apart the two sequences are — and that pairs with near-identical scores on the quantitative metrics behave very differently once clade membership is accounted for. Their resulting three-tier model identified recipients at markedly elevated risk of de novo donor-specific antibody (hazard ratio 6.77, 95% CI 4.64–9.90) and of antibody-mediated rejection (HR 4.41, 95% CI 1.44–13.53), and outperformed the quantitative metrics on the same cohort. The antibody-mediated rejection confidence interval is wide enough to be read as a signal rather than an estimate, and the abstract describes a stratification developed and tested within the same five-centre cohort rather than validated in an independent population, so this is a framework awaiting external replication rather than a calculator ready for the multidisciplinary meeting. What makes it worth a UK consultant's attention now is that British units are actively deciding whether to adopt molecular mismatch load into listing and immunosuppression decisions: if the immunologically meaningful unit turns out to be the clade rather than the count, adopting an eplet-based tool as the definitive risk metric would embed the wrong abstraction at exactly the moment we are choosing one.

### 2. [Association Between Donor HLA-DQ Heterodimers Group and Graft Loss in Kidney Transplant Recipients](https://doi.org/10.1097/TXD.0000000000001998)
[Thivierge MP, Désy O, Aguiar L, Wagner E, Latulippe E, Riopel J, De Serres SA. *Transplant Direct*, 2026. PMID: 42725259.]{.kw-ref}

The companion observation comes from a separate group testing an idea imported from haematopoietic cell transplantation, where patients carrying so-called group 2 DQ heterodimers fare worse, a finding that had been treated sceptically in the absence of a mechanism. The relevant biology is that DQ α1 and β1 chains do not pair freely: group 1 comprises DQA1\*02/03/04/05/06 with DQB1\*02/03/04, and group 2 comprises DQA1\*01 with DQB1\*05/06. Applying that genotype classification to 821 kidney transplant recipients with multivariate survival modelling, the authors found that recipients of a G2G2 donor graft had a 1.9-fold higher risk of graft loss than recipients of a G1G1 graft (95% CI 1.2–2.9, p < 0.01), and that this held independently of donor-recipient mismatch at both HLA-DQ and HLA-DR. Restricting the endpoint to graft loss attributable to biopsy-proven rejection sharpened the estimate considerably, to an adjusted hazard ratio of 4.3 (95% CI 1.1–16.4, p = 0.03), which locates the mechanism in alloimmunity rather than in some unmeasured donor quality variable. Dissecting the G1 genotype by DQB1 allele showed the protective effect was carried specifically by DQB1\*03 alleles — DQ7, DQ8 and DQ9 — with recipients of donors carrying no DQB1\*03 but two DQB1\*05/06 alleles at 2.5-fold higher risk of graft failure than recipients of donors with two DQB1\*03 alleles (95% CI 1.3–4.5, p = 0.01), a gradient that is exactly what one would expect if the effect were biological rather than statistical noise. Sensitivity analyses left the associations intact after adjustment for the conventional predictors of graft loss, though 821 recipients from a single programme with wide confidence intervals on the rejection-specific estimate is a cohort that establishes a signal rather than a threshold for action. Read alongside the Nature Communications paper, the practical significance for UK practice is convergent rather than individual: two independent groups, using different methods on different cohorts, both conclude that the donor's DQ heterodimer identity carries prognostic information that our current mismatch counting — serologic or molecular — discards entirely, and both point towards reporting DQ genotype rather than DQ mismatch burden in the tissue typing report.

### 3. [Predictive Value of Perfusate Cell-free DNA During Hypothermic and Normothermic Machine Perfusion of Donor Kidneys](https://doi.org/10.1097/TXD.0000000000001995)
[Bousnina K, Slagter JS, Fang Y, Boers RG, Boers JB, Heidt S, van IJcken WFJ, Gribnau J, Minnee RC, Hoogduijn MJ, Boer K. *Transplant Direct*, 2026. PMID: 42725188.]{.kw-ref}

If a kidney is going to sit on a pump, the perfusate is free diagnostic material, and cell-free DNA is an attractive candidate because it is released by dying cells and requires no assay development beyond what molecular laboratories already run. This Rotterdam study analysed perfusate from 57 hypothermically perfused and 56 normothermically perfused deceased donor kidneys — the normothermic samples drawn from a randomised trial of two hours of additional end-ischemic perfusion, plus fifteen kidneys declined for transplantation and perfused for research — quantifying nuclear and mitochondrial cell-free DNA separately and, in a subset, sequencing the methylome. At the end of hypothermic perfusion, total cell-free DNA was higher in kidneys that went on to primary non-function (median 0.72 ng/µL, IQR 0.63–0.85) than in those with immediate function (0.48, IQR 0.35–0.58, p = 0.030) or delayed function (0.43, IQR 0.31–0.64, p = 0.031), but the concentration did not survive regression modelling, and the informative signal came instead from the mitochondrial fraction — 28.9-fold more abundant than nuclear DNA — which ran in the opposite direction to intuition, being highest in the kidneys that functioned immediately, with each ten-fold fall in mitochondrial cell-free DNA associated with 25 times higher odds of graft dysfunction (OR 0.040, 95% CI 0.004–0.26, p = 0.017) independent of cold ischaemia time and donor type. During normothermic perfusion the concentration rose steeply across two hours, from a median 0.56 to 10.09 and then 15.80 ng/µL, and again it was the mitochondrial fraction that independently predicted outcome at both one and two hours (at two hours, OR 0.005 per ten-fold increase, 95% CI 0.00001–0.308, p = 0.0067), while kidneys that went on to biopsy-proven rejection within two weeks had substantially higher total cell-free DNA at two hours (36.6 versus 15.2 ng/µL, p = 0.046). The methylome analysis was frankly negative: of 167,840 interrogated regions, 12,611 differed at least two-fold between immediate-function and primary-non-function kidneys but none survived correction for multiple testing, and the five differentially methylated regions recovered by a genome-wide sliding window all sat in intergenic CpG islands, introns or pseudogenes, which the authors concede limits functional interpretation. The inverse direction of the mitochondrial signal is the interesting problem — they suggest abundant mitochondrial DNA may mark a preserved mitochondrial stress response and active turnover rather than irreversible injury, which is a testable hypothesis and also a warning that a crude "more DNA equals more damage" reading would misclassify kidneys in exactly the wrong direction. With 57 and 56 kidneys from one centre, a single end-perfusion sampling point during hypothermic perfusion and no standardisation of isolation or quantification across published series, this is not a clinical assay, but it does tell a UK unit contemplating perfusate biomarkers that fraction and direction must be established before any threshold is set.

### 4. [Effects of End-ischemic Hypothermic Oxygenated Perfusion on 1-y Graft Function in Kidney Transplantation: A Real-world, Single-center Analysis From the United States](https://doi.org/10.1097/TXD.0000000000002005)
[Steggerda JA, Lim T, Kim IK, Todo T, Huang E, Brennan TV, Voidonikolas G, Peng A, Najjar R, Shoji J, Jordan S, Chandran S, Crichton E, Ferrel B, Reyes-Perez J, Alsudaney M, Heeger PS, Wisel SA. *Transplant Direct*, 2026. PMID: 42725207.]{.kw-ref}

Adding oxygen to hypothermic perfusion has European randomised support, and this Cedars-Sinai series is the first US comparative report of an end-ischemic hypothermic oxygenated perfusion programme, covering 279 adult deceased donor kidney-only transplants between December 2023 and March 2025 preserved by static cold storage (137), oxygenated perfusion (56) or non-oxygenated hypothermic perfusion (86). The logistical finding is as important as the functional one: oxygenated kidneys tolerated a median total cold preservation time of 27.9 hours (IQR 23.2–33.9) against 18.3 for static storage and 20.2 for non-oxygenated perfusion (p < 0.001), with a median 12.6 hours of cold ischaemia accumulating before perfusion even began and 21.7% exceeding 36 hours in total, against under 3% in each comparator. At twelve months, median eGFR was 63 mL/min (IQR 44–75) with oxygenated perfusion, 62 with static storage and 53 with non-oxygenated perfusion (p = 0.004 across groups; oxygenated versus non-oxygenated p = 0.019, versus static storage p = 0.96), and the difference persisted in a cohort of donation after circulatory death transplants matched 1:2 on kidney donor profile index and donor and recipient age (22 versus 44 kidneys, 67 versus 48 mL/min, p = 0.034) and among kidneys with more than 18 hours of cold preservation (64 versus 52 mL/min, p = 0.011). Delayed graft function was unaffected, occurring in 48.2%, 51.8% and 54.7% of the three groups respectively (p = 0.75), as was six-month rejection at around 13% throughout. The honest reading requires noting that this was not randomised and that the non-oxygenated comparator carried worse donors — median kidney donor profile index 56% against 43%, donor age 49 against 42 years — although the authors argue the observed eGFR gap substantially exceeds the roughly 3 mL/min per 10% kidney donor profile index that the literature would predict, and they flag their own use of perioperative C1 esterase inhibitor, which was commonest in the worst-performing group, as an unresolved confounder. For UK units, where the binding constraint on accepting a distant or slow-to-allocate kidney is often the clock rather than the organ, the transferable claim is the one about time: oxygenated perfusion delivered function equivalent to straightforward cold storage while absorbing nine extra hours of preservation, which is what converts a declined offer into a transplant, and the authors note it also let them schedule cases out of the small hours and wait for physical crossmatch results in highly sensitised recipients.

### 5. [Machine perfusion distribution across clinical phenotypes in kidney transplantation: A national cohort study using unsupervised clustering](https://doi.org/10.5500/wjt.121821)
[Castellanos De Brigard J, Rangganata E, Papalois VE. *World J Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42751231.]{.kw-ref}

The third preservation paper asks a question no trial can answer — who actually receives a machine-perfused kidney in a national programme, and does perfusion change what the recipient's underlying risk profile predicts — and does so on the UK Transplant Registry itself. The authors took every adult aged 18 to 70 receiving a kidney-only transplant from a deceased donor in the UK between 2014 and 2024, 15,904 cases including 544 with a recorded machine perfusion episode, reduced mixed-type donor and recipient features through a FAMD-like principal component embedding and fitted a Gaussian mixture model, selecting a six-cluster three-component solution from 64 candidates on bootstrap stability, information criterion and minimum cluster size (mean adjusted Rand index 0.784, proportion of ambiguous clustering 0.146). Perfused cases were plainly not distributed at random: cluster 6 — older recipients, hypertensive donors, low behavioural risk, high allocation matchability, locally retrieved organs — held 40.0% of them against 22.9% of the full cohort, while clusters 1 and 4 were under-represented at 7.5% and 6.6%, and the two perfusion modalities segregated differently, hypothermic perfusion falling into clusters 3, 5 and 6 and normothermic into clusters 1 and 4. Five-year graft survival separated the phenotypes sharply in the full cohort, from 93.7% (95% CI 92.6–94.6) in cluster 5 and 91.2% (89.9–92.4) in cluster 3 down to 64.4% (60.6–68.0) in cluster 2, the older comorbid male phenotype with lower-quality donors, and that stratification was retained within the perfused subgroup (log-rank p < 0.001 for both graft and patient survival) — but with two instructive divergences: in perfused cluster 2 patients every graft failure occurred within 2.07 years (16 of 59 patients, median 0.28 years, six on the day of transplant), where full-cohort failures accrued steadily throughout follow-up, and perfused cluster 4 patients showed five-year patient survival of 55.3% against 75.9% in the full cohort. The authors are careful about what this is not: cluster characterisation was post-hoc and descriptive, the perfused subgroup was inside the training data so its stability is face validity rather than validation, recipient BMI and deprivation were 22.6% and 31.2% missing before imputation, and — the caveat with the most operational bite — 544 perfusion episodes across a decade of UK transplants almost certainly reflects incomplete registry capture rather than true practice. That last point is the finding a UK consultant should take away: we are running a national perfusion programme whose denominator we cannot reconstruct from our own registry, and the clinical signal here, that perfusion is being concentrated in one older-recipient phenotype while the sickest phenotype loses its grafts within two years of perfusion, is precisely the kind of thing better data capture would let us interrogate properly.

### 6. [Early Changes in Kidney Transplantation following Implementation of the Increasing Organ Transplant Access Model](https://doi.org/10.2215/CJN.0000001225)
[Husain SA, Levan ML, Thakur M, Reed RD, Locke JE, Weiss SA, Massie AB, Segev DL, Stewart DE. *Clin J Am Soc Nephrol*, 2026. PMID: 42758550.]{.kw-ref}

Transplant policy is rarely randomised, which makes the Increasing Organ Transplant Access model unusually interesting: it is a mandatory US payment experiment in which centres were randomly assigned to participate and then exposed to financial incentives and penalties keyed largely to growth in transplant volume. Using national registry data, the authors ran a difference-in-differences comparison of transplant volume per 30 days across 177 centres — 97 (55%) randomised to participate and 80 (45%) not — contrasting the period before randomisation status was announced with the nine months following implementation. The context matters more than the headline: most centres in both arms, 53% of participants and 55% of non-participants, saw overall transplant volume fall over this period, so what the model produced was a divergence rather than growth. Participating centres recorded a 5% rise in transplant volume per 30 days while non-participants recorded a 3% fall (P = 0.01), and the gap was driven entirely by deceased donor transplants, up 5% among participants against down 9% among non-participants (P < 0.001), whereas living donor volume rose in both arms with no significant difference (+7% versus +19%, P = 0.24). Within the participating centres there was no signal that the response depended on where a centre started: grouping centres by their volume before the model began, by how often they accepted organ offers, or by their transplant rate ratio produced no statistically significant differences in the change achieved. Nine months is a short window, volume is not the same as equitable access or good outcomes, and a model that rewards growth could in principle be satisfied by accepting organs a centre would previously have declined — which the design of this analysis cannot detect. Its relevance to the UK is as evidence rather than as policy: NHS Blood and Transplant operates a national allocation scheme, not centre-level financial incentives, but the inter-centre variation in offer acceptance that motivated this model exists here too, and this is the first randomised evidence that centre behaviour on deceased donor acceptance responds to incentives at all.

### 7. [Mortality and Kidney Failure Risk in HBsAg-Positive Living Kidney Donors: A Retrospective Cohort Study](https://doi.org/10.1111/jebm.70195)
[Yin S, Zhou Y, Huang W, Huang X, Li X, Wu L, Wang X, Lin T. *J Evid Based Med*, 2026. PMID: 42703706.]{.kw-ref}

Hepatitis B surface antigen-positive individuals are increasingly accepted as living kidney donors in high-prevalence settings, and the question this cohort addresses is the one that matters to the donor rather than to the recipient: what happens to a solitary kidney in someone with chronic hepatitis B. The authors compared 128 HBsAg-positive with 1,145 HBsAg-negative living donors over a median 86.0 and 96.0 months of follow-up respectively, using multivariable Cox models for end-stage kidney disease, reduced filtration rate, cancer-specific and all-cause mortality. Serum creatinine rose further in the antigen-positive donors (12.1 versus 8.4 µmol/L, p < 0.001), end-stage kidney disease occurred at 2.94 against 0.58 per 1,000 person-years, and an eGFR below 45 mL/min/1.73 m² at 9.99 against 3.65 per 1,000 person-years, giving a more than doubled adjusted risk of that filtration threshold (HR 2.21, 95% CI 1.06–4.63, p = 0.035). Mortality was 6.85 against 1.4 per 1,000 person-years, and after full adjustment antigen-positive status was an independent predictor of death (HR 7.16, 95% CI 1.71–29.92, p = 0.007) — an estimate whose confidence interval spans a seventeen-fold range and which rests on a small number of events in 128 donors, so the direction deserves more confidence than the magnitude. Stratified analyses are the clinically usable part: e antigen positivity (p < 0.001) and hepatic damage (p = 0.005) marked the donors at higher risk of kidney failure, while receiving antiviral therapy appeared to reduce it (p = 0.004), and propensity-matched sensitivity analyses reproduced the pattern with numerically higher end-stage kidney disease and marginally higher rates of impaired filtration. For UK practice, where HBsAg-positive living donors are uncommon and are assessed individually rather than by protocol, the value is in the counselling arithmetic: these are absolute risks low enough that donation is not categorically precluded, but they are not equivalent to the risks quoted to an uninfected donor, and the effect modification by e antigen status, hepatic injury and antiviral treatment gives a defensible basis for stratifying which prospective donors with chronic hepatitis B can be reassured and which cannot.

### 8. [Skin cancer mortality in Australian and New Zealand kidney transplant recipients: a population-based cohort study using linked health data, 1990-2019](https://doi.org/10.1093/bjd/ljag232)
[Forcey DS, Rosales BM, Wyld ML, De La Mata N, Khosrotehrani K, Webster AC. *Br J Dermatol*, 2026. PMID: 42243641.]{.kw-ref}

That transplant recipients get more skin cancer is textbook; what this linkage study establishes is the shape of the mortality, and it is not the shape most surveillance clinics are built around. Linking the Australia and New Zealand Dialysis and Transplant Registry to both countries' national death registers, the authors followed 21,503 people through 212,317 person-years, counting from a first kidney transplant performed at any point across the three decades to 2019, identifying 251 skin cancer deaths — 82 from melanoma, 169 from keratinocyte cancer — and used indirect standardisation to benchmark the cohort against background population mortality, broken down by sex, by age at the time of death, by decade and by state or country. Absolute skin cancer mortality was 118.2 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 104.1–134.2), comprising 38.6 for melanoma (31.1–48.0) and 79.6 for keratinocyte cancer (68.5–92.6). The standardised mortality ratios are where the clinical message sits: 11.1-fold excess overall, but only 4.5-fold for melanoma against 34.5-fold for keratinocyte cancer — so the cancer that kills transplant recipients disproportionately is the one general dermatology treats as almost never fatal, and it killed twice as many people in this cohort as melanoma did. Excess mortality was present in both sexes, every age group, every residential category and every decade of follow-up, with no evidence that three decades of improving practice have closed the gap, and it tracked ultraviolet exposure, peaking in Queensland (SMR 14.8, 95% CI 11.7–18.8), Western Australia (13.1, 8.7–19.7) and New Zealand (11.0, 8.3–14.6). Death certificate coding by ICD-10 category cannot distinguish squamous from basal cell lineage or capture immunosuppression exposure, and the absolute rates are anchored to some of the highest ambient ultraviolet indices in the world, which limits direct transfer of the numbers to a British cohort. The mechanism is what transfers: the authors call for enhanced surveillance and rapid entry to treatment, and their data argue that a UK post-transplant skin surveillance pathway optimised around detecting melanoma is optimised around the wrong tumour — keratinocyte cancer is the lethal one in this population, and the lethality is in delay.
